newsitem.title: USA: Four nations to discuss Korea in August.
newsitem.headline: Four nations to discuss Korea in August.

text.p: The United States, China, South Korea and North Korea will meet in New York on Aug. 5 to prepare for negotiations to replace the armistice that ended the Korean War with a formal treaty, officials said on Monday.

Senior diplomats from Washington, Seoul and Pyongyang announced after day-long talks that the meeting would discuss and decide procedural matters for the plenary session, including the earliest agreeable date, venue and agenda.

"In a sense, the four-party talks will begin Aug. 5 right here in New York," said a senior U.S. official who asked not to be identified. "We take this as the North Korean commitment to the four-party peace process."

The peace negotiations were first proposed by President Bill Clinton and South Korean President Kim Young Sam in April 1996. Officials from the United States, South Korea and North Korea have met three times, including Monday's gathering, to discuss the possibility of negotiating a peace treaty.

The U.S. official, while almost entirely positive and optimistic about the progress all three sides reported making on Monday, also said: "Although this is a very important step toward those plenary talks, it does not bring us one hundred percent of the way."

Communist North Korea, threatened by famine and with its economy in ruins, agreed in principle in April to join the peace talks but linked its participation to food aid and an end to U.S. trade sanctions.
In a statement, U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright welcomed Pyongyang's decision to take part.
"The purpose of the four-party talks is to reduce tensions and build confidence on the Korean peninsula with the aim of putting a formal end to the hostilities of the Korean War," she said.
The armistice ended the fighting, but technically not the Korean War of 1950-53 that pitted the communist North backed by China against the South, which was supported by the United States.
A senior South Korean official told reporters that Washington and Seoul had received the prior consent of China to announce the August gathering once the timing was agreed.

The U.S. official said the role of China and the other three countries had yet to be defined, but he remarked that "the Chinese have told us they are very interested in joining these talks and so I expect that they would make a contribution."

North Korean Vice Minister of Foreign Affairs Kim Gye Gwan told reporters that Monday's meeting was important in creating "a good atmosphere" for the forthcoming talks. He declined to comment on the details other than a joint statement by U.S., South Korean and North Korean officials.
North Korea raised the question of food aid again in Monday's meeting as it had done in previous discussions, U.S. and South Korean officials said.

South Korean Ministry of Foreign Affairs official Yu Myung Hwan said North Korea wanted Washington and Seoul to commit a specific amount of food aid before they would come to the preparatory talks. He said Washington and Seoul declined to link pledges of food aid with the peace talks.

Political analysts say Pyongyang has agreed to join the four-way talks in a policy shift designed to hold the reclusive state together. They say the Stalinist government needs to repair its relationship with Western countries who could provide much-needed assistance.
